transcript.text: Samsung RS68A8820S9/EU flashing 22E on the display and the fridge side isn't as cold as it should be. What does 22E mean and can I fix it?

22E is a fridge evaporator-fan error: the appliance is not detecting the internal fan running as it should. That fits a fridge compartment that is not cold enough, because this fan moves cold air through the appliance. The usual causes are ice stopping the fan blade, a failed fan motor, or less commonly a wiring/control fault; a defrost fault can create the ice in the first place. You can safely check the easy cause first: make sure food and packaging are not covering the air vents inside the fridge, then leave the doors shut for a few hours. Is the freezer side still properly cold (about -18°C), and are those fridge vents clear? If the freezer is cold but the fridge remains warm with 22E showing, it is likely to need an engineer to inspect the fan and any ice/defrost problem rather than simply replacing a part blindly.
Freezer side is fine and the vents aren't blocked. Fridge is reading 9C with very weak airflow from the vents. No burning smell or tripping either.

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. With the freezer still cold, the fridge at 9°C and only weak airflow, this is much more likely to be an air-circulation fault than a general cooling-system failure. A failed fan motor is also possible; a wiring or control fault is less common. Please check for an unusual frost or ice patch on the rear panel inside the fridge, around the air outlets—do not remove internal panels. Heavy frost points to a defrost-related ice build-up; no frost makes the fan motor or its electrical supply more likely and would usually need an engineer to diagnose and repair.
There's a bit of frost around the vent at the top back of the fridge. I haven't taken any panels off and won't. What should I do next?

The sensible next step is a complete manual defrost. The 22E code is a fridge-fan fault code, and frost at the vent can be enough to impede the fan or airflow; a full defrost is the safe way to distinguish ice from a failed fan. 1. Switch off and unplug the appliance, move chilled food to cool boxes, and put towels around it.
2. Leave both doors open for 24–48 hours so hidden ice can fully melt; do not chip ice or remove internal panels.
3. Dry it thoroughly, restart it, set the fridge to about 3–5°C, and keep the doors closed as much as possible while it cools. If it cools and the code clears but frost/22E returns within days or weeks, an engineer will need to check the evaporator fan and automatic-defrost components. If 22E remains straight after the full defrost and the fridge still does not cool, the fan motor or its wiring/control is more likely and also needs an engineer.
Ok, I did the full defrost with the doors open. The code cleared and the fridge cooled down fine, but 22E came back about 10 days later. What now?

The full defrost temporarily restoring cooling and clearing 22E, followed by the code returning in about 10 days, points to recurring ice build-up rather than a one-off blockage. Most likely, an automatic-defrost component has failed—typically the defrost heater, sensor/thermal protection or control circuit—so ice builds up again and interferes with the fridge evaporator fan; the 22E may be the fan being unable to run properly as a result. A worn or gapped door seal can also feed in moist air and speed this up, so please inspect the seal closely without dismantling anything. If it looks sound, book a fridge engineer: internal panel removal and testing of the fan and defrost components is needed, rather than another repeated manual defrost or buying a fan blindly.
[Helpful to see: image "Fridge not cooling — simple checks first" — Before suspecting the sealed system, check the temperature setting, that the door seal closes cleanly, that there's air space and clean condenser coils at the back, and listen for the compressor. Unplug before cleaning at the back. A sealed-system or refrigerant repair is a job for a qualified engineer. Typical layout — your model may differ.]
